function getParameterByName(name, url) {
		if(url == null){
		  url = window.location.href;
		}
	    name = name.replace(/[\[\]]/g, '\\$&');
	    var regex = new RegExp('[?&]' + name + '(=([^&#]*)|&|#|$)'),
		results = regex.exec(url);
	    if (!results) return null;
	    if (!results[2]) return '';
	    return decodeURIComponent(results[2].replace(/\+/g, ' '));
	}

	String.prototype.replaceAll = function(str, newStr){
		// If a regex pattern

			return this.replace(str, newStr);
		}
		// If a string
		return this.replace(new RegExp(str, 'g'), newStr);

	function getCookie(cname) {
	 	var name = cname + "=";
  		var decodedCookie = decodeURIComponent(document.cookie);
		var ca = decodedCookie.split(';');
  		for(var i = 0; i <ca.length; i++) {
    			var c = ca[i];
    			while (c.charAt(0) == ' ') {
     				 c = c.substring(1);
    			}
    			if (c.indexOf(name) == 0) {
    				 return c.substring(name.length, c.length);
    			}
  		}
  		return "";
	}

	var referer = "";//sessionStorage.container;
	var pcontainer = sessionStorage.getItem("container");
	var searchResultsPagePath = "";
	if(((pcontainer) && pcontainer.indexOf('Prisma')!=-1)){
	    referer = 'Prisma' ;
	}        
        else if(((pcontainer) && pcontainer.indexOf('Cortex')!=-1)){
            if( pcontainer.indexOf('CloudCortex') != -1){

                referer = 'Cortex' ;
            }

function callMainSitePrismaNavHTML(){
    
    var referrer_domain = 'https://www.paloaltonetworks.com';
    sessionStorage.setItem("domain",referrer_domain);
    if(referer == 'Prisma'){
        //var menu_url = referrer_domain+'/_jcr_content/globals/cleanHeaderPrisma.prismaRenderer.html';
        var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/unit-nav-renderer.php?type=prisma&domain=en';
        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/search/prismasearch";
        }
    if(referer == 'CloudCortex'){
        var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/unit-nav-renderer.php?type=cortexcloud&domain=en';
        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/search/cortexcloudsearch";	
    }
    if(referer == 'Cortex'){
        //var menu_url = referrer_domain+'/_jcr_content/globals/cleanHeaderCortex.cortexRenderer.html';	
        var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/unit-nav-renderer.php?type=cortex&domain=en';	
        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/search/cortexsearch";	
    }
    if(referer == 'Sase'){
        //var menu_url = referrer_domain+'/_jcr_content/globals/cleanHeaderSase.saseRenderer.html';
        var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/unit-nav-renderer.php?type=sase&domain=en';
        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/search/sasesearch";
    }
    if(referer == 'Unit'){
        var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/unit-nav-renderer.php?type=unit42&domain=en';
        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/content/pan/en_US/search/unit42search";
		    }
    if(referer == 'Ngfw'){
        //var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/ngfw-cdss-nav-renderer.php';
        var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/unit-nav-renderer.php?type=ngfw&domain=en'; 
        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/search/ngfwcdsssearch";
    }
    if(referer == 'Idira'){
        //var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/ngfw-cdss-nav-renderer.php';
        var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/unit-nav-renderer.php?type=idira&domain=en'; 
        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/search/idirasearch";
    }
    httpGet(menu_url,'menu_html');
    document.getElementById('main-nav-menu-cont').removeAttribute("style");
}
function addStyle(styles) {            
    /* Create style document */
    var css = document.createElement('style');
    css.type = 'text/css';

    if (css.styleSheet) 
        css.styleSheet.cssText = styles;
    else 
        css.appendChild(document.createTextNode(styles));

    /* Append style to the tag name */
    document.getElementsByTagName("head")[0].appendChild(css);
}
function httpGet(theUrl,req_type) {
    if (window.XMLHttpRequest) { // code for IE7+, Firefox, Chrome, Opera, Safari
        xmlhttp=new XMLHttpRequest();
    } else {// code for IE6, IE5
        xmlhttp=new ActiveXObject("Microsoft.XMLHTTP");
    }
    xmlhttp.onreadystatechange=function()
    {
        if (xmlhttp.readyState==4 && xmlhttp.status==200)
        {
            if(req_type == 'menu_html'){
            var nav_text = xmlhttp.responseText.replaceAll('https://static.cloud.coveo.com/searchui/v2.9159/js/CoveoJsSearch.Lazy.min.js', '');
            nav_text = nav_text.replaceAll('src="/', 'src="'+maindomain_lang+'/');
            nav_text = nav_text.replaceAll("src='/", "src='"+maindomain_lang+"/");
            nav_text = nav_text.replaceAll("'/content", "'"+maindomain_lang+"/content");
                        
            document.getElementById("PAN_2021_NAV_ASYNC").innerHTML = nav_text.replaceAll('href="/', 'href="'+maindomain_lang+'/');

            var lozad_back = document.getElementsByClassName('lozad-background');
            Array.prototype.forEach.call(lozad_back, function(el) {
            // Do stuff here
            var el_back_img_path = el.getAttribute('data-background-image');
            var first_pos = el_back_img_path.indexOf("'");
            var last_pos = el_back_img_path.indexOf("'",first_pos+1);
            el_back_img_path = el_back_img_path.substring(first_pos+1,last_pos);
            let result = el_back_img_path.includes(main_site_url);
            if(result == false){
                el.setAttribute("data-background-image",main_site_url+el_back_img_path);
            }
            else{
                el.setAttribute("data-background-image",el_back_img_path);
            }
            });
            const observer_lozad = lozad('.lozad, .lozad-background'); // lazy loads elements with default selector as '.lozad'
            observer_lozad.observe();
            }
            if(req_type == 'head_inline_css'){
            addStyle(xmlhttp.responseText);
            }
        }
    }
    xmlhttp.open("GET", theUrl, true );
    xmlhttp.send();    
}    
    
if(referer == 'Prisma' || referer == 'CloudCortex' || referer == 'Cortex' || referer == 'Sase' || referer == 'Unit' || referer == 'Ngfw' || referer == 'Idira'){
    const article = document.querySelector('#PAN_2021_NAV_ASYNC');
    if(referer == 'Prisma'){
        article.dataset.type = 'prisma';
        $('#PAN_2021_NAV_ASYNC').removeClass('default').addClass('defaultRedesigned');
    }

        article.dataset.type = 'cloudcortex';
    }
    else if(referer == 'Cortex'){
        article.dataset.type = 'cortex';
    }
    else if(referer == 'Sase'){
        article.dataset.type = 'sase';
    }
    else if(referer == 'Unit'){
        article.dataset.type = 'unit';
    }
    else if(referer == 'Ngfw'){
        article.dataset.type = 'ngfw';
    }
    else if(referer == 'Idira'){
        article.dataset.type = 'idira';
    }
    //set class to default
    if(referer == 'Unit' || referer == 'Ngfw'){
        $('#PAN_2021_NAV_ASYNC').removeClass('default').addClass('defaultRedesigned');
    }
    callMainSitePrismaNavHTML();
}

              <h1>The Permanent Threat: Analyzing Aeternum’s Blockchain-Based C2 Operations and Communications</h1>
              <div class="ab__video">
              <span class="duration">

              <div class="be__contents-wrapper">
                <h2><a id="post-185207-_4lt92rr5muov"></a>Executive Summary</h2>
<p>Aeternum is a recently discovered C++ botnet loader that shifts its command-and-control (C2) infrastructure entirely to the public Polygon blockchain. Instead of relying on centralized servers or domains, threat actors operate Aeternum by writing encrypted and plaintext instructions directly using smart contracts. A smart contract is a self-executing program stored on a blockchain that automatically runs when specific conditions are met.</p>
<p>Infected devices continuously query public remote procedure call (RPC) endpoints to retrieve and execute these on-chain commands.</p>
<p>The Aeternum botnet uses decentralized networks and evasion techniques, such as virtual machine detection and antivirus scanning, to operate effectively. This combination establishes a highly resilient, low-cost threat that complicates existing law enforcement takedown methods.</p>
<p>In this article, we analyze three malware cases linked to the Aeternum botnet:</p>
<ul>
<li>Aeternum’s loader, C2 and downloader communications</li>
<li>Related Python-based malware using the Telegram API for C2</li>
<li>A blended threat consisting of XWorm RAT, the XMRig cryptocurrency miner and data exfiltration</li>
</ul>
<p>Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed in this article through the following products and services:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/wildfire" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced WildFire</a></li>
<li><a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/advanced-url-filtering" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced URL Filtering</a> and <a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/dns-security" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced DNS Security</a></li>
<li><a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/ngfw" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Next-Generation Firewall</a> with <a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/advanced-threat-prevention/administration" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced Threat Prevention</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/cortex/cortex-xdr?_gl=1*13pmp8e*_ga*NzQyNjM2NzkuMTY2NjY3OTczNw..*_ga_KS2MELEEFC*MTY2OTczNjA2MS4zMS4wLjE2Njk3MzYwNjEuNjAuMC4w" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cortex XDR</a> and <a href="https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/resources/datasheets/cortex-xsiam-aag" target="_blank" rel="noopener">XSIAM</a></li>
</ul>
<p>If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the <a href="https://start.paloaltonetworks.com/contact-unit42.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Unit 42 Incident Response team</a>.</p>
<table style="width: 100%;">
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="width: 35%;"><b>Related Unit 42 Topics</b></td>

<h2><a id="post-185207-_g0xb9fkx2s3"></a>Background on Aeternum</h2>
<p>This article builds upon research by the Ctrl-Alt-Intel team on the <a href="https://ctrlaltintel.com/research/Aeternum-Part-1/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Aeternum C2 architecture</a> and the <a href="https://ctrlaltintel.com/research/Aeternum-Part-2/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">loader binary</a>. That previous research primarily focused on host-based activity.</p>
<p>This malware advertises itself as Aeternum C2 BotNet Loader, and security researchers call it either <a href="https://qrator.net/blog/details/Exploring-Aeternum-C2/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Aeternum C2</a> or Aeternum loader.</p>
<p>Our analysis focuses on three malware samples associated with Aeternum activity. Our first sample is the Aeternum loader.</p>
<h2><a id="post-185207-_4uydhvjk86km"></a>Sample One: Aeternum Loader</h2>
<p>SHA256 hash: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">5bfb25b8255b61e5ffdf6804451534bcfa9f1dfd225e6c8cdcefb5f50d846898</span></p>
<h3><a id="post-185207-_r9axxjxnqqe5"></a>Sample Characteristics</h3>
<p>This Aeternum loader sample is named <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Build.exe</span>. It is the initial UPX-packed 32-bit portable executable (PE) Windows malware file compiled in C++. Its primary functions are to establish a persistent presence, perform reconnaissance and communicate with the decentralized Polygon blockchain to retrieve encrypted C2 commands.</p>
<h3><a id="post-185207-_j7jwlt4dlh4x"></a><strong>Behavioral Analysis</strong></h3>
<p>The overall flow of this sample executes in multiple stages:</p>
<ol>
<li>Initial execution and self-unpacking
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-alpha;">
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Build.exe</span> executes a multi-stage self-unpacking sequence</li>
</ol>
</li>
<li>Persistence and setup
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-alpha;">
<li>Creates a folder under the user's <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">AppData\Local</span> directory and copies itself to it</li>
<li>Creates a Windows shortcut under the program menu's Startup directory (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Wmi_Framework_APIKEY_wmsnet_&lt;random_value&gt;.lnk</span>) to ensure auto-launch upon reboot</li>
<li>Executes supporting binaries (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">wmiframework.exe, ZrvEsJQzWQ.exe, STAAAAAS.exe</span>)</li>
</ol>
</li>
<li>Configuration retrieval and network communications
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-alpha;">
<li>Deobfuscates global configuration data to produce parameters used to construct network endpoint strings</li>
<li>Sends JSON-RPC requests to Polygon RPC endpoints (decentralized C2 communication)</li>
<li>Queries immutable <a href="https://dcentwallet.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/4413887286671-What-is-a-smart-contract-address" target="_blank" rel="noopener">smart contract addresses</a> using the contract method <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">0xb68d1809</span> to retrieve encrypted C2 commands</li>
<li>Decrypts the payload using a weak PBKDF2HMAC/AES-GCM routine</li>
</ol>
</li>
<li>Downloader and payload execution
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-alpha;">
<li>Downloads files as instructed by the C2 server, such as a clean <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">putty.exe</span> and the malicious <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">DotNetZip.dll</span>, from GitHub repositories</li>
<li>Executes the malicious DLL, which uses hard-coded credentials to connect to a Telegram C2 bot (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">DLLSendC2Bot</span>)</li>
</ol>
</li>
<li>Exfiltration
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-alpha;">
<li>Packages the stolen information for exfiltration over encrypted channels to trusted domains, code-hosting platforms and the Telegram API</li>
</ol>
</li>
</ol>
<h3><a id="post-185207-_taafsur9s1zm"></a>Static Deobfuscation (XOR)</h3>
<p>The pattern of encryption keys for the Aeternum loader (i.e., <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">\x00\x00\x00[ENC bytes]\x00[KEY bytes]\x00\x00\x00</span>) consists of:</p>
<ul>
<li>Three null bytes followed by the encrypted payload bytes</li>
<li>A null byte, followed by the key bytes</li>
<li>Three null bytes</li>
</ul>
<p>Since the pattern is known, a script can identify the different number of occurrences along with its offsets. When found, we can then use the key to deobfuscate the hidden information.</p>
<p>Figure 1 shows two examples of the decryption process against two different obfuscated string matches and their deobfuscated values. These values consist of the JSON object strings used for HTTP-based C2 communication during the execution of the malware and its subsequent interaction with the Polygon blockchain.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185208" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185208" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185208 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-359953-185207-1.png" alt="A screenshot of a command line interface displaying SSH key exchanges and messages labeled 'Push 133' and 'Push 232'" width="1000" height="130" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-359953-185207-1.png 1224w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-359953-185207-1-786x102.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-359953-185207-1-768x100.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185208" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 1. Deobfuscated (XOR) blockchain RPC request Information.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Additional deobfuscated strings also include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Polygon RPC endpoints (i.e., <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">hxxps[:]//polygon-mumbai-bor-rpc.publicnode[.]com</span>)</li>
<li>File extensions (.e.g, <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.ps1, .dll, .exe</span>)</li>
<li>HTTP header information (i.e., <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">User-Agent</span>)</li>
<li>C2 command information (e.g., <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">hwid, args, ping</span>)</li>
<li>Smart contract method (i.e., <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">0xb68d1809</span>)</li>
</ul>
<p>However, we suspect that this particular sample differs from others, since we did not find the smart contract addresses either through deobfuscation or plain-text pattern search. During network analysis, this sample used 22 different smart contract addresses during C2 communications.</p>
<p>The full table of deobfuscated strings can be found in the Indicators of Compromise section of this article.</p>
<h3><a id="post-185207-_6ad2djocuemn"></a><strong>Network Traffic</strong></h3>
<p>The Aeternum loader performed the following activities as part of its downloading and C2 communications:</p>
<ul>
<li>Communicating with the Polygon blockchain network</li>
<li>Downloading files from GitHub repositories</li>
<li>Interacting with social media via Telegram’s API (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">api.telegram[.]org</span>)</li>
</ul>
<p>Figure 2 shows an example of the communications traffic filtered in Wireshark.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185219" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185219" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185219 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-361878-185207-2.png" alt="A screenshot of Aeternum C2 and downloader activity log showing multiple entries of HTTP requests. Details include timestamps, ports, protocols, hosts, and request methods. " width="1000" height="393" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-361878-185207-2.png 1396w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-361878-185207-2-786x309.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-361878-185207-2-768x302.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185219" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 2. Aeternum C2 and downloader network traffic activity.</figcaption></figure>
<h4><a id="post-185207-_lon85rzh9p5f"></a>Aeternum Polygon Blockchain C2 Communications</h4>
<p>This section explores how Aeternum performed C2 communications on the Polygon blockchain and how it uses different smart contract addresses to retrieve C2 commands.</p>
<h5><a id="post-185207-_qy9e96uwpsyw"></a>Polygon’s JSON-RPC (HTTP Request Analysis)</h5>
<p>This sample made a <a href="https://www.jsonrpc.org/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">JSON-RPC</a> request using HTTP to the Polygon blockchain. Figure 3 shows the TCP stream of an HTTP POST request to the Polygon RPC endpoint, which includes a JSON object with two important fields: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">to</span> and <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">data</span>. The <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">to</span> field contains the contract address, and the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">data</span> field contains the Polygon contract's <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">getDomain()</span> method <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">0xb68d1809</span>.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185230" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185230" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185230 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-364793-185207-3.png" alt="A screenshot of Wireshark displaying HTTP stream details. It shows HTTP headers and payload in hexadecimal and ASCII formats. Red annotations point to a &quot;32 byte offset,&quot; &quot;266 byte length,&quot; &quot;payload starts,&quot; and &quot;padding&quot;." width="1000" height="901" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-364793-185207-3.png 2048w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-364793-185207-3-488x440.png 488w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-364793-185207-3-777x700.png 777w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-364793-185207-3-768x692.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-364793-185207-3-1536x1384.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185230" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 3. Example of Aeternum C2 blockchain HTTP communication (request and response).</figcaption></figure>
<h5><a id="post-185207-_u75zh1azvz9y"></a>Polygon’s JSON-RPC (HTTP Response Analysis)</h5>
<p>Following the JSON-RPC request, if the RPC response is an HTTP 200 OK, it will include a JSON object containing the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">result</span> field with its corresponding payload. This is structured with the following byte sequence:</p>
<ul>
<li>Offset (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">0x20</span> = 32 bytes)</li>
<li>Payload length (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">0x10a</span> = 266 bytes)</li>
<li>Payload (variable values)</li>
<li>Padding (variable length)</li>
</ul>
<h4><a id="post-185207-_kuo4anbz2eqk"></a>Weak Encryption Implementation</h4>
<p>Building on existing research, we observed that Aeternum implements a substandard encryption scheme. Specifically, it uses a self-salting password.</p>
<p>The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) considers a self-salting password a critical cryptographic flaw via predictable salt and public key derivation source, in their remediation standard: <a href="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/132/final" target="_blank" rel="noopener">NIST SP 800-132</a>. This oversight allows the decryption of the malicious payload by using two known variables: the smart contract address and the payload.</p>
<p>The main decryption logic corresponds to the following operations:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>PBKDF2HMAC (key stretching):</strong> This function uses the SHA256 algorithm to repeatedly hash the password, using the password itself as the salt</li>
<li><strong>Key derivation: </strong>The <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">kdf.derive(password)</span> performs the key derivation. It takes the encoded password and transforms it into a high-entropy 32-byte (256-bit) cryptographic key.</li>
<li><strong>Advanced Encryption Standard in Galois/Counter Mode (AES-GCM) initialization:</strong> The derived key is used to initialize an AES/GCM object</li>
<li><strong>Decryption:</strong> The decryption of the ciphertext uses the provided initialization vector (IV) and the payload, resulting in a UTF-8 encoded string</li>
</ul>
<p>We used a <a href="https://github.com/ctrlaltint3l/intelligence/blob/main/Aeternum%20Loader/aeternum_c2_command_decrypt.py" target="_blank" rel="noopener">custom Python script</a> to automate the decryption process, which expects the two values passed to it: the contract address and the hex-string payload, as mentioned above. Figure 4 shows the results of this script run on an encrypted Aeternum blockchain value.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185241" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185241" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185241 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-369870-185207-4.png" alt="A screenshot of a command prompt window displaying encrypted text and a Python decryption process. The text includes contract address details and a GitHub URL, ending with a process marked &quot;SUCCESS!&quot; with an address and iterations noted." width="1000" height="571" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-369870-185207-4.png 1204w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-369870-185207-4-770x440.png 770w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-369870-185207-4-768x439.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185241" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 4. Decryption script run on an encrypted Aeternum blockchain value.</figcaption></figure>
<p>In this case, the decrypted string contains the Aeternum command <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">all:url:<em>&lt;URI for </em>putty.exe<em>&gt;</em></span>, which is a command used to instruct the botnet to proceed and fetch the target file.</p>
<p>Although the analyzed sample uses encryption, we found additional samples using plain-text C2 commands, as well as an unknown encrypted payload.</p>
<h4><a id="post-185207-_9509msrbstfi"></a>Aeternum Downloader Activity</h4>
<p>The malware download requested two different files, <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">putty.exe</span> and <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">DotNetZip.dll</span>, as Figure 5 below shows.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185252" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185252" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185252 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-372483-185207-5.png" alt="&quot;A screenshot of a network log featuring requests made to GitHub. The log displays columns for Time, TCP Port, Protocol, Host, and Info. The Info column includes file paths and HTTP request methods like GET." width="1000" height="117" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-372483-185207-5.png 1851w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-372483-185207-5-786x92.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-372483-185207-5-768x90.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-372483-185207-5-1536x179.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185252" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 5. Aeternum downloader activity.</figcaption></figure>
<p>While investigating the malware’s downloader activity, we found requests for file artifacts hosted on GitHub in two different Github projects. Figure 6 shows the malicious DLL in an October 2025 commit from one repository.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185452" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185452" style="width: 786px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185452 size-medium lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Figure-6-786x135.png" alt="A screenshot of a file explorer showing a folder titled &quot;1&quot; containing a file with a size of 49 KB. A note below states, 'Binary file not shown'." width="786" height="135" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Figure-6-786x135.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Figure-6-1920x331.png 1920w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Figure-6-768x132.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Figure-6-1536x265.png 1536w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Figure-6.png 1944w" sizes="(max-width: 786px) 100vw, 786px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185452" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 6. Malicious DLL file hosted on GitHub.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The hosted <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;"><a href="https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/12498d4e4bf07747a9a52d6803d3211fd731ded6473b41cf4795ac56947d0366" target="_blank" rel="noopener">putty.exe file</a> </span>is a copy of a legitimate installer for PuTTY version 0.83. The <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;"><a href="https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/1505eda3da68e2ff9919b55a31018bd30a991236f041aee835f3bc4e430ce505" target="_blank" rel="noopener">DotNetZip.dll file</a></span> is a malicious DLL file.</p>
<p>While this Aeternum loader sample retrieved legitimate files like PuTTY, this is likely for testing. Attackers could easily swap files in these repositories for malware using the same filename, instantly compromising the safety of anyone who downloads them.</p>
<h3><a id="post-185207-_iw9rekzh4d3w"></a>Exfiltration via the Telegram API: Aeternum</h3>
<p>After successfully downloading <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">DotNetZip.dll</span> from GitHub and executing it, the malware sample initiated new communications to an endpoint at Telegram’s API (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">api.telegram[.]org</span>).</p>
<p>As a DLL, the malware's entry point <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">DllMain()</span> first checks for a specific condition by comparing <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">fwReason</span> to 1 to confirm it is being called. Then it invokes the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">CollectAndSendSystemInfo()</span> function, as shown below in Figure 7.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185274" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185274" style="width: 800px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185274 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-377393-185207-7.png" alt="A screenshot of disassembled code in a software analysis tool. The image shows function details and call flow of the code. The main function displayed calls another function named CollectAndSendSystemInfo. There are annotations indicating exported entries and attributes, with arrows displaying the sequence of calls." width="800" height="595" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-377393-185207-7.png 725w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-377393-185207-7-592x440.png 592w" sizes="(max-width: 800px) 100vw, 800px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185274" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 7. Disassembled code from the malicious DLL.</figcaption></figure>
<p>This function is in charge of all the information gathering and data exfiltration from the compromised machine. The most notable information about this sample is its lack of obfuscation or encryption, as both the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">chat_id value</span> (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">-4991861036</span>) and the bot’s API token (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">8305917772:AAHAou...</span>) are hard-coded, as Figure 8 shows in the disassembled code.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185285" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185285" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185285 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-379428-185207-8.png" alt="A screenshot of a disassembled code snippet from a software analysis tool. The code includes labeled memory addresses, assembly instructions like &quot;push&quot; and &quot;mov,&quot; and data reference. " width="1000" height="676" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-379428-185207-8.png 1656w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-379428-185207-8-651x440.png 651w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-379428-185207-8-1035x700.png 1035w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-379428-185207-8-768x519.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-379428-185207-8-1536x1039.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185285" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 8. Hard-coded <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">chat_id</span> value and Telegram bot API token.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Once the malware has collected all the information, it constructs an HTTP request to exfiltrate the information. The structure of this HTTPS request through the Telegram API follows:</p>
<ul>
<li>HTTP Method
<ul>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">POST</span> (submission of the collected information)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Base path and bot token
<ul>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">/bot</span> prefix (required for all Telegram bot API calls)</li>
<li>Concatenated bot API token (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">8305917772:AAHAou…</span>)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>API Method (URI path)
<ul>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">/sendDocument</span> (tells Telegram what action the bot should perform. In this case, it is attempting to send a file (e.g., PDF, ZIP) to a chat)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Protocol
<ul>
<li>HTTP/1.1 (indicates the version of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol being used for the communication)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>HTTP Headers
<ul>
<li>User-agent (set to <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">SystemInfo Bot/2.0</span>)</li>
<li>Content-Type (set as <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">multipart/form-data</span> with a boundary set as <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">systeminfoboundary</span>)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>HTTP Request Body
<ul>
<li>Form-data, containing the names:
<ul>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">chat_id</span> (The unique identifier for the target chat)</li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">caption</span> (Text to accompany the file)</li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">document</span> (The file to be sent, which in this case is a PNG file named <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">screenshot.png</span>)</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p>The content of the exfiltrated information contains different information from the compromised machine, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>CPU</li>
<li>RAM</li>
<li>Disk</li>
<li>GPU</li>
<li>Administrator rights check</li>
<li>Windows User Account Control (UAC) status</li>
</ul>
<p>Figure 9 shows an exfiltration request revealed using Burp Suite that contains an example of the data collected by the malware sample.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185296" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185296" style="width: 700px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185296 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-382718-185207-9.png" alt="A screenshot of a &quot;POST&quot; request sent to a Telegram server. The details include connection information, user-agent, and content type. The system information shows the OS as Windows 10 Enterprise, CPU as Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-3470, and memory status with 1.9GB available out of 8GB. Other technical details about proxy and wireless configurations are visible." width="700" height="1066" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-382718-185207-9.png 627w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-382718-185207-9-289x440.png 289w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-382718-185207-9-460x700.png 460w" sizes="(max-width: 700px) 100vw, 700px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185296" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 9. Data exfiltration through the Telegram bot API.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The text in the image is in Russian (i.e., <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">ДОПОЛНИТЕЛЬНАЯ ИНФОРМАЦИЯ</span>, which translates to <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Additional Information</span>) and uses Cyrillic characters, which require specific encodings like UTF-8 to properly decode.</p>
<h2><a id="post-185207-_tbibaz8203yp"></a>Sample Two: XWorm + XMRig CoinMinder + Data Exfiltration</h2>
<p>SHA256 hash: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">f2a326cff405299e4ebdfaac955c52fc7e496544eaa0921ecad4816cb3ae3a27</span></p>
<p>Pivoting on characteristics of the first sample, we found several matches using specific patterns based on the smart contract method function (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">0xb68d1809</span>). Among these, we identified a 64-bit Windows PE sample that leverages the Aeternum botnet to simultaneously drop an XWorm binary, an XMRig cryptocurrency miner and a data exfiltrator.</p>
<p>The sample is named <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">XBinderOutput_protected.exe</span> and written in C/C++. This PE file is a PyInstaller-packed application containing a Python 3.14 script named <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">XBinderOutput_protected_temp.py</span>.</p>
<p>The embedded script implements multi-layer cryptographic decryption using ChaCha20, AES-CTR and AES-CBC to recover an encrypted payload. The payload is then written to the temporary directory as <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">esewurmgvbqt.exe</span> and executed with a hidden window. The script includes anti-analysis checks for virtual machine environments and debugger presence.</p>
<p>Like the previous sample for Aeternum loader, once executed, this second sample made a JSON-RPC request using HTTP to the Polygon blockchain containing Aeternum’s <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">to</span> and <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">data</span> values. An HTTP <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">200 OK</span> response was returned as expected, indicating that a command payload was found and its content returned. Figure 10 shows an example of this traffic.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185307" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185307" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185307 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-384747-185207-10.png" alt="A screenshot of a Wireshark window showing an HTTP POST request. The window displays headers and raw data and specific details. There are fields like &quot;content-type: application/json&quot; and &quot;x-frame-options: SAMEORIGIN.&quot; The bottom shows options for filtering and export, with a search button labeled &quot;Find text." width="1000" height="808" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-384747-185207-10.png 2048w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-384747-185207-10-545x440.png 545w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-384747-185207-10-867x700.png 867w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-384747-185207-10-768x620.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-384747-185207-10-1536x1241.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185307" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 10. Polygon’s blockchain JSON-RPC request and response.</figcaption></figure>
<p>This time, the hexadecimal value response is not encrypted but converts directly to plain text. After translating the hexadecimal values to ASCII, we found a Pastebin URL as noted below in Figure 11.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185318" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185318" style="width: 900px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185318 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-388910-185207-11.png" alt="A hexadecimal data table with offset values on the left and decoded text on the right. The decoded text includes a URL among other characters." width="900" height="246" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-388910-185207-11.png 1542w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-388910-185207-11-786x215.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-388910-185207-11-768x210.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-388910-185207-11-1536x420.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 900px) 100vw, 900px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185318" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 11. Decoding Aeternum’s C2 command.</figcaption></figure>
<p>This URL contains the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">/raw/</span> URI path that is designed to return the data as-is, without any further processing by the service. Thus, the malware has less work to do in terms of parsing or processing the retrieved information. This URL returned configuration data for the XMRig cryptocurrency miner.</p>
<p>After the malware retrieved data from the Pastebin URL, it started two binaries it had dropped to the infected host, one for an <a href="https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/4e24bbd0fabac6c3efcec943046afbfd332b2c0108a13becfda23a0e26f9ff5f" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Xworm</a> client and one for an <a href="https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/81bb80d9c5a97dc41b65f6248c131963c91346eb4fb672836b3d53ae67564d9f" target="_blank" rel="noopener">XMRig cryptocurrency miner</a>.</p>
<h3><a id="post-185207-_b3punwycj0ad"></a>XMRig CoinMiner Analysis and Configuration</h3>
<p>The Pastebin URL returned the XMRig cryptocurrency miner configuration data as a JSON object containing different fields. These fields included mining-based settings such as:</p>
<ul>
<li>Algorithm</li>
<li>API-endpoint</li>
<li>Max CPU</li>
<li>Password</li>
<li>Pool</li>
<li>Wallet address</li>
</ul>
<p>It also included two behavior-based options:</p>
<ul>
<li>The <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">stealth-target</span> option that enables evasive behavior by blocklisting system monitoring utilities. It triggers a process suspension and its related mining activity upon the execution of diagnostic tools (e.g., Process Hacker) to mask the miner’s footprint and resource consumption.</li>
<li>The <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">kill-targets</span> option that implements process termination as a persistence and resource-optimization strategy. It identifies and kills active processes associated with endpoint security software and distributed computing programs to prevent system remediation and ensure maximum CPU allocation for the miner.</li>
</ul>
<p>The associated Pastebin URL occasionally returns different data for the XMRig conﬁguration. Despite these changes, the data structure remains identical. Figure 12 displays an example of the XMRig configuration data seen in June 2026.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185329" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185329" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185329 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-391407-185207-12.png" alt="A screenshot of a programming code snippet displayed in a browser window on the pastebin.com website. The code includes parameters for a mining pool, password, and other configurations such as keepalive, SSL, and API endpoints. It lists processes and stealth targets related to a server setup." width="1000" height="730" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-391407-185207-12.png 1990w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-391407-185207-12-603x440.png 603w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-391407-185207-12-959x700.png 959w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-391407-185207-12-768x560.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-391407-185207-12-1536x1121.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185329" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 12. Pastebin XMRig cryptocurrency miner configuration structure.</figcaption></figure>
<h3><a id="post-185207-_w0titv3rt7wd"></a>XWorm RAT Analysis and Network Activity</h3>
<p>In addition to the XMRig cryptocurrency miner, the main sample dropped an XWorm client named <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">XWormclient.exe</span>. This filename is the default name used when using the XWorm v7.4 builder, indicating that the author generated and bound it into the malicious package.</p>
<p>We extracted the Xworm sample's configuration using CAPE’s community <a href="https://github.com/CAPESandbox/CAPE-parsers/blob/main/cape_parsers/CAPE/community/XWorm.py" target="_blank" rel="noopener">parser for XWorm</a>. This dump of information contains configuration information as shown below in Figure 13, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>Version of the builder (XWorm v7.4)</li>
<li>Mutex</li>
<li>C2 server</li>
<li>IP address</li>
<li>Port</li>
<li>Key</li>
</ul>
<figure id="attachment_185340" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185340" style="width: 700px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185340 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-394103-185207-13.png" alt="A command prompt window showing a script execution. The details include various IP addresses, ports, and paths. Mentions of &quot;Python,&quot; &quot;CAPE,&quot; and &quot;USB&quot; are visible." width="700" height="199" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185340" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 13. XWorm configuration extraction using the CAPE parser.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Armed with this information, specifically the C2 server key, C2 communication port and XWorm version values, we tricked the sample into connecting to a controlled instance of the matching XWorm panel version. Figure 14 shows a screenshot of the C2 panel after the XWorm sample connected to our controlled instance.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185351" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185351" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185351 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-395964-185207-14.png" alt="A screenshot of XWorm V7.4, with open windows displaying system information and processes. Details include IP addresses, usernames, and software versions, with CPU and RAM usage at the top." width="1000" height="519" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-395964-185207-14.png 933w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-395964-185207-14-786x408.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-395964-185207-14-768x398.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185351" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 14. XWorm bot panel controlling a compromised host.</figcaption></figure>
<h3><a id="post-185207-_ohcb4uhogqqz"></a><strong>Data Exfiltration From the Compromised Host</strong></h3>
<p>During the final stage of this Aeternum sample's execution, the injected system process starts an information gathering and encryption process.</p>
<p>Figure 15 shows an outbound connection HTTP POST request to a C2 server at <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">193.221.200[.]219</span> with a custom user-agent (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">cpp-httplib/0.18.3</span>) and JSON values containing two keys with Base64-encoded values.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185362" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185362" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185362 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-398023-185207-15.png" alt="A screenshot of a Wireshark interface displaying HTTP stream data. The window shows a POST request to an API endpoint with headers, including content type and user agent details, followed by JSON data containing encoded information. The interface includes options for data representation and search functions at the bottom." width="1000" height="595" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-398023-185207-15.png 2048w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-398023-185207-15-739x440.png 739w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-398023-185207-15-1176x700.png 1176w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-398023-185207-15-768x457.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-398023-185207-15-1536x914.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185362" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 15. HTTP C2 exfiltration with base64-encoded data.</figcaption></figure>
<p>After further analysis and reverse engineering to understand the meaning of those two keys, we discovered that the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">uqhash</span> value contains an AES-128 encryption key. We also discovered the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">data</span> value contains the exfiltrated data in an encrypted blob form.</p>
<p>The following section explains the encryption details and the decryption process we followed to reveal the exfiltrated information.</p>
<h4><a id="post-185207-_8jlk0d6pn27m"></a>Encryption Routine</h4>
<p>The encryption routine takes raw input bytes and pads them with 0x00 until the length is a multiple of 16 bytes. It then derives a fixed 16-byte key by truncating or zero-extending the provided hexadecimal input. The data is processed block-by-block using a 16-byte block cipher in Electronic Code Book (ECB) mode, producing a deterministic ciphertext where each block is independently encrypted. The result is written out without any IV, chaining or authentication, closely matching a typical minimal malware-style encryption wrapper.</p>
<p>The encryption routine has the following characteristics:</p>
<ul>
<li>Algorithm used: AES-128 (16-byte block cipher) in ECB mode</li>
<li>Key properties: no IV, deterministic output, zero padding (non-standard), identical plaintext blocks → identical ciphertext blocks</li>
<li>Context in this test: binary data from a file is padded and encrypted in-place using a fixed 16-byte key derived from CLI hexadecimal input, mimicking a simple malware/configuration protection routine</li>
</ul>
<h4><a id="post-185207-_4wufy8ezjjsr"></a>Decryption Routine</h4>
<p>To decrypt the required information, we developed a script to reverse the encryption process identified during our analysis and reverse engineering. This script takes two parameters:</p>
<ol>
<li>The encrypted payload file dump</li>
<li>The hexadecimal representation of the Base64-decoded AES-128 key as a single concatenated string</li>
</ol>
<p>Figure 16 shows the execution of the decryption script, which in this case generated a 580-byte data dump.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185373" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185373" style="width: 800px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185373 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-401731-185207-16.png" alt="A screenshot of a terminal window displaying a Python decryption command. It shows the file path and commands with input and output file details. " width="800" height="156" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185373" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 16. Automated payload decryption using a Python script.</figcaption></figure>
<p>By viewing the contents of the output file, the exfiltrated data is revealed as shown below in Figure 17.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185384" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185384" style="width: 900px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185384 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-403488-185207-17.png" alt="A screenshot of a terminal window displaying the decryption process of an encrypted file. Information includes status code, computer name, username, hash rate, pool details, CPU specifications, client details, and other technical parameters." width="900" height="171" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-403488-185207-17.png 859w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-403488-185207-17-786x149.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-403488-185207-17-768x146.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 900px) 100vw, 900px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185384" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 17. Decrypted Information exfiltrated to the C2 server.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Certain behavior (i.e., drop of a <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.sys</span> file) and network patterns (e.g., URI path, JSON object attributes) match with ZingoStealer <a href="https://blog.talosintelligence.com/haskers-gang-zingostealer/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">reported by Cisco Talos</a> on April 13, 2022. However, we cannot fully attribute this activity to ZingoStealer.</p>
<h2><a id="post-185207-_u0ba8xw8s3vi"></a>Sample Three: Python Malware Source Code Analysis</h2>
<p>SHA256 hash: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">ea1b6ff3a0c1a749b9f09d66789973321d63d8896b48f7345193bdad512950a2</span></p>
<h3><a id="post-185207-_yf51y4jx1tif"></a><strong>Python Source Code Analysis</strong></h3>
<p>Our third sample is a Python script file containing the source code for the Aeternum malware. The key element used to confirm its association with the Aeternum operation is the data value <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">0xb68d1809</span>, which functions as the unique function selector used to query the Polygon smart contract.</p>
<p>The code contains a blockchain-based fall-back mechanism to counter infrastructure takedowns. By executing a read-only <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">eth_call</span> to a specific Polygon smart contract, the malware can retrieve and decrypt new C2 domains on the fly. This decentralized dead-drop resolver, combined with the Star Drop space-themed Telegram formatting, highlights an operation designed for resilience and stealth. Figure 18 below shows a section of the Python script illustrating this.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185395" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185395" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185395 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-405460-185207-18.png" alt="A screenshot of Python code defining a function. It includes JSON-RPC request setup, error handling with response checks, and data conversion for domain retrieval. The code retrieves and decodes a domain, highlighting text processing and exception handling." width="1000" height="742" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-405460-185207-18.png 1334w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-405460-185207-18-593x440.png 593w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-405460-185207-18-943x700.png 943w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-405460-185207-18-768x570.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185395" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 18. The <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">get_domain()</span> function used to retrieve C2 domains from the smart contract.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Analysis of the malware’s source code reveals a multi-staged infection chain that begins with a social engineering lure impersonating a <a href="https://dbeaver.io/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">DBeaver</a> installer. To ensure it only executes on high-value targets, the code includes rigorous anti-analysis routines that check for specific sandbox usernames, machine names and a minimum of 8 GB of RAM.</p>
<p>Notably, it validates the presence of <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Zone.Identifier</span> alternate data streams in a user account's <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Downloads</span> folder to confirm the system is not a pristine, empty virtual machine. Once validated, the malware establishes persistence by creating a disguised shortcut in the Windows Startup folder and employs an <a href="https://github.com/AbdouRoumi/Early_Bird_APC_Injection" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Early Bird APC injection</a> technique.</p>
<p>This technique involves spawning a suspended, signed binary (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">dpapimig.exe</span>) and injecting shellcode into its address space, effectively executing the malicious payload before security hooks are fully initialized. Figure 19 below shows a section of the Python script representing this.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185406" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185406" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185406 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-407913-185207-19.png" alt="A screenshot of a code snippet written in Python. It features lists of usernames and computer names, as well as checks for system information such as platform use and RAM size. The code includes functions and conditional statements, and the name &quot;dbeaver&quot; is mentioned as a build." width="1000" height="622" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-407913-185207-19.png 1397w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-407913-185207-19-707x440.png 707w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-407913-185207-19-1125x700.png 1125w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-407913-185207-19-768x478.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185406" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 19. Block-listed user and computer names with memory check.</figcaption></figure>
<h3><a id="post-185207-_epm4b5veyrwj"></a>Exfiltration via the Telegram API: Python Source Code</h3>
<p>The source code further details an aggressive focus on cryptocurrency data exfiltration. It features hard-coded routines to harvest credentials from over 55 cryptocurrency browser extensions and 10 popular desktop wallets. Data exfiltration and C2 communication are handled via a hybrid architecture.</p>
<p>While primary reconnaissance is sent via Telegram, the main C2 loop uses obfuscated JSON payloads padded with junk data to break traffic signatures. Figure 20 below illustrates this in a section of Python script.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185417" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185417" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185417 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-410598-185207-20.png" alt="A screenshot of a Python script for web scraping and automation. The code retrieves the computer name, IP address and gathers system information like OS platform and Windows Defender status. It also initializes a Telegram bot communication and attempts to scrape extensions and wallet information. The script utilizes libraries such as &#96;os&#96;, &#96;platform&#96;, and &#96;requests&#96;." width="1000" height="748" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-410598-185207-20.png 1434w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-410598-185207-20-588x440.png 588w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-410598-185207-20-936x700.png 936w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-410598-185207-20-768x575.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185417" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 20. The <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">send_tg()</span> function used for data exfiltration via Telegram.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The full table of the malware indicators can be found in the Indicators of Compromise section of this article.</p>
<h3><a id="post-185207-_e3iinns2mdl7"></a>Blockchain Reconnaissance</h3>
<p>The key to tracking the Aeternum botnet lies in the Polygon smart contract's function selector, <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">0xb68d1809</span>, which resolves to the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">getDomain()</span> function. The malware calls this public function to retrieve an XOR key and Base64-encrypted C2 domain stored in the contract's storage slot. The permanence of this 4-byte selector across all Aeternum malware samples provides a reliable cryptographic fingerprint, which ties all related activity back to the same campaign.</p>
<p>The smart contract architecture is simple but resilient, using storage slot 0 for the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">admin</span> (deployer's wallet) address and slot 1 for the encrypted <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">domain</span>. While the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">getDomain()</span> function is public for malware retrieval, a second critical selector, <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">0xb249cd2d</span> (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">updateDomain</span>), is an admin-only function used to rotate the C2 domain. Transactions linked to the primary operator's smart contract address, associated with the moniker LenAI, confirmed they actively use this <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">updateDomain()</span> method to push new C2 information, such as <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">hxxps[:]//cdnjsdelivr[.]beer/</span>, to the blockchain.</p>
<p>Figure 21 below shows a flowchart of this operation.</p>
<figure id="attachment_185428" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-185428" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-185428 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-413138-185207-21.png" alt="A flowchart illustrating a security breach pattern. Two nodes labeled &quot;updateDomainA&quot; lead to the same destination. One transition shows encrypted code leading to &quot;getDomainA&quot;. The other shows code leading to the same endpoint. The endpoint displays a red bug icon, symbolizing a vulnerability or malware." width="1000" height="187" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-413138-185207-21.png 2048w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-413138-185207-21-786x147.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-413138-185207-21-1920x359.png 1920w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-413138-185207-21-768x144.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-image-413138-185207-21-1536x287.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-185428" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 21. Aeternum blockchain operation.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Static analysis of the Ethereum virtual machine (EVM) bytecode from all three samples indicates a single threat group is iteratively refining the codebase. Despite variations in deployment addresses and sequential compiler upgrades (from <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">solc 0.8.0 to 0.8.30</span>), the contracts maintain an identical state-management architecture and share the three fundamental function selectors (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">0xb249cd2d, 0xb68d1809 and 0xf851a440</span>).</p>
<p>These technical details, including progressive <a href="https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9569819" target="_blank" rel="noopener">gas optimization</a> and updated error messages, prove attackers are refining and redeploying this same codebase over time. This establishes Aeternum as an evolving threat infrastructure.</p>
<h2><a id="post-185207-_fyqdarmqm0z8"></a>Conclusion</h2>
<p>The Aeternum botnet is one of the latest threats leveraging blockchain-based botnets. Attackers are migrating from conventional self-hosted C2 mechanisms to more evasive and resilient alternatives. They are hiding malicious payloads in smart contracts, such as those on the Polygon blockchain, a trend exemplified by Aeternum.</p>
<p>This investigation shows that malware developers are leveraging the blockchain as a decentralized communication mechanism for their operations. They are also leveraging Aeternum as a botnet selection for the C2 management console. We expect this trend to continue.</p>
<p>Throughout the duration of this study, our Advanced Threat Prevention security solution successfully identified and recorded more than 29,000 detection events (as of June 4, 2026).</p>
<p>Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed above through the following products and services:</p>
<ul>
<li>The<a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/wildfire" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Advanced WildFire</a> machine-learning models and analysis techniques have been reviewed and updated in light of the indicators shared in this research.</li>
<li><a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/advanced-url-filtering" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced URL Filtering</a> and <a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/dns-security" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced DNS Security</a> identify known domains and URLs associated with this activity as malicious.</li>
<li>The <a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/ngfw" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Next-Generation Firewall</a> with the <a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/advanced-threat-prevention/administration" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced Threat Prevention</a> security subscription can help block the attacks with best practices via the following Threat Prevention signature/s: <a href="https://threatvault.paloaltonetworks.com/?query=87116" target="_blank" rel="noopener">87116</a>, <a href="https://threatvault.paloaltonetworks.com/?query=87152" target="_blank" rel="noopener">87152</a>.</li>
<li><a href="https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/cortex/cortex-xdr?_gl=1*13pmp8e*_ga*NzQyNjM2NzkuMTY2NjY3OTczNw..*_ga_KS2MELEEFC*MTY2OTczNjA2MS4zMS4wLjE2Njk3MzYwNjEuNjAuMC4w" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cortex XDR</a> and <a href="https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/resources/datasheets/cortex-xsiam-aag" target="_blank" rel="noopener">XSIAM</a> help to prevent the threats described in this article, by employing the <a href="https://docs-cortex.paloaltonetworks.com/r/Cortex-XDR/Cortex-XDR-4.x-Documentation/Malware-protection" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Malware Prevention Engine</a>. This approach combines several layers of protection, including <a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/wildfire" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced WildFire</a>, Behavioral Threat Protection and the Local Analysis module, to prevent both known and unknown malware from causing harm to endpoints.</li>
</ul>

<script>
 var PAN_LOAD_RECAPTCHA_LANGUAGE = 'en_US';

(function($) {
	// Migrated from the unit42-v5 + Modifications
	var subscribeSuccess = false;
	var email = document.getElementById('newsletter-email');
	var subscription_form = document.getElementById('unit42footerSubscription_form');
	var subscription_form_button = document.getElementById('unit42footerSubscription_form_button');
        var isCaptchaComplete02  = false;	
        window.captchaInlineFormOnload = function(token){
            isCaptchaComplete02 = true;
            $("form[name='Unit42_Subscribe'] button[id='unit42footerSubscription_form_button']").prop('disabled', false);
        }
        var PAN_INLINE_FORM_RECAPTCHA_LOADED = false;
        const SITE_KEY = '6LdDKhIsAAAAABdoYV3PR5VJ2Gz23_dLSvq2uvBQ'; 
                if(!PAN_INLINE_FORM_RECAPTCHA_LOADED){
               PAN_INLINE_FORM_RECAPTCHA_LOADED = true;
               // trigger loading api.js (recaptcha.js) script
               var recapthaScript = $("script[src='https://www.google.com/recaptcha/enterprise.js?render="+SITE_KEY+"&hl="+PAN_LOAD_RECAPTCHA_LANGUAGE+"&onload=captchaInlineFormOnload']").length
               // console.log("recapthaScript",recapthaScript);
               if (!recapthaScript) {
                   var head = document.getElementsByTagName('head')[0];
                   var script = document.createElement('script');
                   script.typerecapthaScript = 'text/javascript';
                   script.src = "https://www.google.com/recaptcha/enterprise.js?render="+SITE_KEY+"&hl="+PAN_LOAD_RECAPTCHA_LANGUAGE+"&onload=captchaInlineFormOnload";
                   head.appendChild(script);
               }
               else{
                   captchaInlineFormOnload();
                }
           }
            	
	
	$(subscription_form).submit(function(e) {
		e.preventDefault();
		e.stopImmediatePropagation();
		updateEmailMask();
		var success = true;
		var form = $(this);
		var mail = form.find('input[name="Email"]');
		
		if (mail.val() === '') {
			mail.addClass('has-error');
			showError(1);
			success = false;	
		}  else if (!isEmail(mail.val())){
			showError(2);
			success = false;
		}
		else {
			mail.removeClass('has-error');
			$('.error-mail').addClass('d-none');
		}

		

		if (success) {
                                                if(grecaptcha){
                        grecaptcha.enterprise.ready(function() {
                            grecaptcha.enterprise.execute(SITE_KEY, {action: 'submit'}).then(function(token) {
                                submitSubscribeForm({token :token, action : 'submit'},form);
                            });
                        });
                    }
                    			
		}
		return false;
	});
        function submitSubscribeForm(tokenData, form){
            var serialized_data = form.serialize();
            let captchaParams = `&g-recaptcha-response=${tokenData.token}&action=${tokenData.action}`;
            $.ajax({
				type: 'POST',
				url: form.attr('action'),
				data: serialized_data+captchaParams,
				beforeSend: function() {
                 form.find('button').addClass('is-loading');
    			},
				success: function(msg) {
					form.find('.form-success-message').html('<p class="success-message">You have been successfully subscribed</p>');
					form.find('button').removeClass('is-loading');
					$(email).val('');
					clearError();
				},
				error: function(jqXHR, textStatus, errorThrown) {
					$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled', true);
					form.find('button').removeClass('is-loading');
					
				}
			});
            
        }
	function showError(error_type){
		if(error_type == 1) {
			$('.error-mail').text("Please enter the email address.").addClass('error-show');
			$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled');
		} else if(error_type == 2){
			$('.error-mail').text("Please provide a valid e-mail address.").addClass('error-show');
			$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled');
		}	
		$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-loading');
	}
	function clearError(){
		$('.error-mail').text("").removeClass('error-show');;
		$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-loading');
		$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-disabled');
	}
	
	$(email).on('input', function (event) { 
		var email = $(this).val();
		if (isEmail(email) ) {			
			clearError();
		} else if(email == ""){
			clearError();
		} else{
			showError(2);			  
		}
    });

	function isEmail(email) {
		var re = /^(([^<>()\[\]\\.,;:\s@"]+(\.[^<>()\[\]\\.,;:\s@"]+)*)|(".+"))@((\[[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\])|(([a-zA-Z\-0-9]+\.)+[a-zA-Z]{2,}))$/;
		return re.test(String(email).toLowerCase());
	}
	
	
	
	function updateEmailMask() {
		var email = $("#unit42footerSubscription_form input[name='Email']").val();
		if (email && email.trim() != '') {
			var maskedEmail = maskEmailAddress(email);
			$("#unit42footerSubscription_form input[name='emailFormMask']").val(maskedEmail);
		}
	}

	function maskEmailAddress (emailAddress) {
		function mask(str) {
			var strLen = str.length;
			if (strLen > 4) {
				return str.substr(0, 1) + str.substr(1, strLen - 1).replace(/\w/g, '*') + str.substr(-1,1);
			}
			return str.replace(/\w/g, '*');
		}
		return emailAddress.replace(/([\w.]+)@([\w.]+)(\.[\w.]+)/g, function (m, p1, p2, p3) {
			return mask(p1) + '@' + mask(p2) + p3;
		});

		return emailAddress;
	}

}(jQuery));
//# sourceMappingURL=main.js.map
	
</script>

<script type="text/javascript">
	$(document).ready(function(){
		$("html").on("click", ".language-btn", function () {
			$(this).toggleClass("expand");
			$(".language-dropdown").toggleClass("expand");
		});

		$("html").on("click", "body", function (b) {
			if (!$(b.target).is(".language-btn")) {
				$(".language-btn").removeClass("expand");
				$(".language-dropdown").removeClass("expand");
			}
		});
	});
</script>

	var isProcessing = false; 
    function alter_ul_post_values(obj,post_id,ul_type){
	
		if (isProcessing)    
		return;  
		isProcessing = true;   
		var like_nonce = jQuery('#_wpnonce').val();
		jQuery(obj).find("span").html("..");
                jQuery.ajax({
                    type: "POST",
                    url: "https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/plugins/like-dislike-counter-for-posts-pages-and-comments/ajax_counter.php",
                    data: "post_id="+post_id+"&up_type="+ul_type+"&ul_nonce="+like_nonce,
                    success: function(msg){
                            jQuery(obj).find("span").html(msg);
                            isProcessing = false; 
                            jQuery(obj).find('svg').children('path').attr('stroke','#0050FF');
                            jQuery(obj).removeClass('idc_ul_cont_not_liked idc_ul_cont_not_liked_inner');
                    }
 		});
	}

function noSell(event) {
    event.preventDefault();
   if (( typeof OneTrust != 'undefined') &&  (!!OneTrust)) {
       OneTrust.ToggleInfoDisplay();
    }else{
      var href = event.target.getAttribute('href');
        window.open(href, '_blank'); 
    }
}

function loadScript(url, defer){
    var script1 = document.createElement('script');
    script1.setAttribute('type', 'text/javascript');
    script1.setAttribute('src',url);
    if(defer == true){
        script1.setAttribute('defer','defer');
    }
    document.head.appendChild(script1);
}
function loadScript1(url, callback){

    var script = document.createElement("script")
    script.type = "text/javascript";
    if (script.readyState){  //IE
        script.onreadystatechange = function(){
            if (script.readyState == "loaded" || script.readyState == "complete"){
                script.onreadystatechange = null;
                callback();
            }
        };
    } else {  //Others
        script.onload = function(){
            callback();
        };
    }
    script.src = url;
    document.getElementsByTagName("head")[0].appendChild(script);
}
if(referer == "CloudCortex" || referer == "Prisma" || referer == "Cortex" || referer == "Sase" || referer == "Unit" || referer == "Ngfw" || referer == "Idira"){

    }, 3000);
	}
}

document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function() {
  // Find all the forms on the page
  var forms = document.getElementsByTagName("form");

  // Loop through each form
  for (var i = 0; i < forms.length; i++) {
    var form = forms[i];

    // Check if the hidden input field already exists
    var requestInput = form.querySelector("input[name='web_unit42_req_id']");
    if (!requestInput) {
      // Create a hidden input element if it doesn't exist
      requestInput = document.createElement("input");
      requestInput.type = "hidden";
      requestInput.name = "web_unit42_req_id";
      requestInput.id = "web_unit42_req_id";

      // Append the hidden field to the form
      form.appendChild(requestInput);
    }
  }
});

// Assign the onCheqResponse function to the window object to handle events from any form
window.onCheqResponse = function(encryptedMessage, requestID) {
  // Find all the forms on the page
  var forms = document.getElementsByTagName("form");

  for (var i = 0; i < forms.length; i++) {
    var form = forms[i];
    var requestInput = form.querySelector("input[name='web_unit42_req_id']");
    if (requestInput) {
      requestInput.value = requestID;
    }
  }
};
